speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. What basis of fact is there in the report that French authorities have taken some Canadian rifles from Algerian rebels?

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman was good enough to give me notice yesterday of his intention to ask this question and also to indicate the magazine from which his information was received. I wish to thank him for that notice because it has given us time to get in touch with the government concerned in order to ascertain whether or not this report is accurate.
We have not yet received that report, and therefore I cannot answer his question definitively. The article in question includes information which the writer received from a French official in Algeria to the effect-and this is the information he gave the writer- that out of every ten rifles taken perhaps eight are British and the others Canadian or Belgian. I do know that an examination of the trade statistics going back to 1946 reveals no shipments of rifles from Canada to Spanish Morocco, French Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia or Egypt during that period, but, as I have stated, I cannot give a final reply until I have heard from the government concerned with this matter.

The short answer to this question is that the government of the federal republic of west Germany has at no time contributed toward the maintenance of Canadian troops in that country. Canadian forces were not sent to Germany as occupying forces but as a part of Canada's contribution to the defence forces of the North Atlantic alliance. It has always been the government's policy to pay the cost of maintaining these forces. The only financial support that has been received from the government of the federal republic of west Germany has been in respect of capital expenditures such as the construction of barracks and airfields. The major construction program for the Canadian defence forces in Germany has now been mainly completed and no major additional projects are contemplated in the near future.
No official confirmation has been received of the reports appearing in the press to the effect that the German finance minister has stated that it is not the intention of the federal republic to continue to contribute to the financial support of such forces, and it is not clear from the present press reports whether the financial support extends to capital expenditures such as barracks and airfields which are, of course, of some interest to Canada.

That meeting was held some weeks ago and one of the bankers was asked for his opinion and he told the meeting that if a farmer could not get a bank loan under ordinary circumstances with his credit rating he was not likely to get one under the government plan.
I think that is fairly significant of the attitude the banks have taken. Another matter in which we are going a little bit offside is that too many people think that $1,500 is involved in these loans. The bankers are not going to take any chances in connection with the security for the loans they make. This banker went on to say that the applicant would have to list all his debts, including chattel mortgages, and disclose his net worth. The items to be disclosed would be whether

or not his land taxes were unpaid. If so, the applicant would have to obtain a clearance. Some of the municipalities are allowing exemptions of from $1.50 to $2.50 per acre. As I say, it has been argued that it is that type of farmer who is going to benefit under this legislation.
This whole question came up at a meeting in Saskatoon where farm union officials gathered to discuss this whole question, and some very revealing figures came out which I should like to quote. It was stated that a quarter section farmer with 155 acres under cultivation would be able to deliver 1,085 bushels of wheat. Based on a 7-bushel quota the value of that wheat as No. 2 would be $1.18 per bushel at the local elevator, or a total of $1,280. Assuming a loan on the basis of 50 per cent would give you $640. But the value of 300 bushels already delivered would be $354, and 320 bushels under an additional 2-bushel quota would be $365. When those amounts are deducted you have a maximum loan of $21. This is one of the farmers the Minister of Trade and Commerce says he is really concerned about, says he is really going to help. That takes care of the quarter section farmer.

The figures I was quoting were not the compilation of figures made up after the legislation was introduced. This was a survey that was made in anticipation of what the legislation, if and when it appeared, was going to do. So I shall refrain from reading from that particular article. I have other figures I shall use, and I shall accept responsibility for them.
I pointed out what this legislation is going to do for the quarter-section farmer. He is not going to be able to borrow any money. As a matter of fact, he has $21 too much to start with. In the case of the half-section farmer, his maximum borrowing power would be $1,280, but if he had deliveries of 300 bushels under the initial quota he would then be eligible for a loan not exceeding $194.70. Again, this is the type of farmer the Minister of Trade and Commerce is so much concerned about. He is going to suffer if this legislation does not pass post-haste. Now let us turn to the three-quarter-section farmer, and I feel that is the ceiling when we are speaking about small holdings. We find that he is in an even worse position than the other two. Because of added expenses and his capital investment, he of necessity would need to get a considerably greater amount than either of the two I mentioned earlier, but under this legislation this farmer

will receive only $84. When we consider that all of the grain we have been able to market on the prairies to date represents a complete and dismal crop failure, anything a farmer has been able to deliver above 15 bushels an acre he can consider a little better than a complete crop failure. So it is not hard to point out that this legislation, in so far as helping the small prairie producer is concerned, falls far short of anything that he had expected.
Now I should like to deal for a moment with another aspect of this legislation, and here, I feel, is the nub of the whole question. I believe that the best arguments as to why this legislation should not be passed are to be found in the very arguments put up by the government as to why it should be passed.
I should like to deal with that aspect for a few moments. I hope you will not rule me out of order, Mr. Speaker, when I quote the minister himself in this connection. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking in this debate, had this to say, as recorded on page 602 of Hansard:
The present legislation is designed to deal with a different problem, a problem which arises from the superabundant production of grain on the prairies during recent years.
Then he goes on to quote figures to prove that there has been superabundant production. He gives figures showing that in the years 1947 to 1950 the average yearly production on the prairies was 361 million bushels, in that five-year period. He then points out that in the last five years, from 1951 to the present time, production has averaged 515 million bushels. In other words, the average production increased during those five years by 154 million bushels. Further on he said that we have had increased marketing as well. He went on to quote figures showing that in the five-year period prior to 1951 the average marketings were 223 million bushels per year, and from 1951 to the present time he said our marketings have averaged 312 million bushels per year. In other words, the average yearly marketings during the past five years have been 89 million bushels greater per year than in the previous five years.
What exactly is the minister saying? I think it is quite an amazing revelation, because in effect this is what the minister is saying. Farmers will become bankrupts when
(a)	they produce better than average crops,
(b)	they are able to market better than average marketings. This is an amazing statement. If there was ever a greater indictment of the agricultural policies of this government, I have never heard it. I think it is a serious matter when we have the

I am not disputing his figures. I am not disputing the fact that we have had the equivalent of five very large crops in 3 years, but it is very serious that in the face of that the farmers' economic position is steadily but surely deteriorating. I do not know why the government does not face up to the realities of the situation, because after all it is an entirely different matter, to say we are producing more and we are marketing more than it is to say the farmers' net position is such and such.
What is the farmers' actual economic position? I should like to quote figures published by the research section of the Department of Agriculture. For the year 1953 the cash income-not the net income, because we are unable to get the net figures-of prairie farmers was $1,448,749,000, but in 1955 the cash income of prairie farmers had fallen to $961,518,000, a drop of $487,231,000 in two years.
Yesterday I received a publication from the dominion bureau of statistics which verified the figures I have quoted. It is a serious matter when in two years you have a drop in the farmer's cash income of 66-5 per cent. In addition to that, in the same period, costs have risen by 66 per cent. It is difficult to say what the farmer's net position would be if we had those figures. I am amazed at the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), although in some respects I am not because we have known him to do things like this before in order to prove a point. I am sure that if the story were made known to Liberal members opposite they would take a different view of their position. In order to suppress any fears some Liberal members might have as to what the exact position of the western farmer is, he quoted precisely the same figures as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) quoted in this house to prove that the farmer has never been as well off in his life before. In order to spike it, he quotes the pool. I refer to Hansard, of February 10. After he had quoted all of those figures on incomes of all kinds to show that the farmer has so much money he does not know what to do with it, then he has this to say for the benefit of the members of the government as reported at page 1060 of Hansard of that date:
And so, as the wheat pool says In Regina there has not been any going down of farm income on farms in general across Canada: the farm income has been higher year by year.
I think that is a serious accusation in the face of the figures produced by the minister's own department. The three prairie pools have completely repudiated the minister in this respect. Recently they published a memorandum indicating that the income of Canadian farmers had dropped for the third successive year. They go on to say that all across Canada farm income has dropped by some 2 [DOT] 1 per cent, but in the prairie provinces this drop has been to the extent of nearly 28 per cent. It is obvious that in trying to make a case for this legislation the government is using every method at their disposal to discourage any fears that might arise in the minds of their own supporters.
I should like to deal for a moment with some of the other arguments, some of the other alibis that have been used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to why we should support this milk and water legislation. I am not going to delay the house with a long dissertation on parity prices or cash advances, but I should like to say this. There was a great deal of misinformation given to the house when we were discussing cash advances. It was said that could not be done; it was not feasible. In order to support his argument against cash advances, the minister went to some length to cite the United States support program as it applied to cash advances on farm-stored grain. He said that the government of the United States would not accept ownership of the grain until it was stored in government storage. Well, of course, that is completely fantastic. They do nothing of the kind. They pay the farmer up to a certain percentage on grain stored in government approved storage on the farm. All these arguments are nothing but red herrings drawn across the trail in an attempt to prove this cash advance proposition is completely unworkable.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we are still going to be faced with an acute economic problem on the prairies regardless of whether or not this legislation is passed. I would even go farther and say that even if this legislation were going to help or even if bank loans were rejected and cash advances were made, it would still not solve tfie agriculture crisis which we have been facing in western Canada for a good many years and which we will be facing for a good many years to come. This crisis will not be solved unless this government is prepared to completely overhaul its agriculture policy. Cash advances, bank loans, all of these things are only bits and pieces and by themselves mean absolutely nothing in so far as stabilizing agriculture is concerned. Only when all of these things

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Grain
are welded together in a comprehensive agriculture policy will these bits and pieces really mean anything. I am convinced that in the very near future the government will be forced to undertake the implementation of a complete agriculture policy to stabilize the farm industry in this country. I might say also that one of the planks of that policy will be the acceptance of the principle of cash advances on farm-stored grain without interest and administered through the wheat board.
Before I move on, I should like to mention the argument that those who are opposing bank loans are in effect trying to undermine the wheat board. I am very much surprised that the government is making such a case for the wheat board. If they were as interested in the maintenance of the wheat hoard as they are trying to make out, why do they not put that board on a permanent basis? Why do they not put all grains grown in western Canada under the wheat board? If they would do that, then they would be proving that they are interested in the wheat board. We would not have today the spectacle out in southern Manitoba of United States farmers coming across the border, without any restrictions, and delivering flax into the elevators' or loading it into box cars that are badly needed for grain grown in that area. Now, that is the situation we have today because the government has not seen fit to place flax and rye under the jurisdiction of the wheat board. I think it is a deplorable situation when box cars are so scarce and elevator space is so badly needed.
So, Mr. Speaker, I would just conclude by saying that this legislation is not going to benefit the people the Minister of Trade and Commerce is telling us it is intended to help. It is not going to help anyone. It did not do the job before and it will not do the job now. It is wrong in principle. It is wrong in practice, and for that reason we cannot accept it.

I did speak a couple of times at the resolution stage, but on both occasions I spoke for less than half an hour and therefore I make no apology for speaking at this time. I rise mainly for the purpose of clarifying the stand of this group on this bill and on the amendment.
Whilst the question of advances against grain held on the farm is an important one, it is not the farmers' No. 1 headache today. The No. 1 headache from which the farmers are suffering today is the fact that they are in a price-cost squeeze. Lack of advances to farmers in many cases merely aggravates that situation. It does so in varying degrees. In so far as the farmer who is in a fairly strong position is concerned, it is merely

an inconvenience. Unfortunately there are not many farmers in that happy position. The majority of the farmers have no large reserves upon which to fall back. It is not merely the small farmer who is handicapped. There are today many large farmers with large holdings of land who have heavy obligations, who are in the process of paying for machinery and for their land. Even though they are large farmers, these farmers today are suffering under a severe handicap.
I would say that the failure of the government to take action today to halt the fall in farm income and the failure to support farm prices at an adequate level constitutes a flagrant breach of faith with the farmers of this country. It is breaking a definite pledge that was made by the government in the latter years of the war; it was a pledge that was made by the prime minister of this country to the people of Canada. I think the farmers of this country have the right to expect something better than that from this government when the pledge was made by the prime minister at that time. The pledge was in words to this effect: In view of the fact that the farmers during the latter years of the war were having to take for their commodities prices that were less than the world market price, the government would after the war stabilize farm prices to compensate them for that loss. On wheat alone that loss amounted to half a billion dollars. If you take into consideration the losses as a result of selling all farm produce at less than world market prices in the latter years of the war and in the early post-war years, there would be several more hundreds of millions of dollars to add to that loss of $500 million. I therefore say that the failure of the government today to maintain farm prices at a level that bears a fair relationship to the price of other commodities constitutes a flagrant breach of faith having regard to the promise they made to the farmers in the latter years of the war.
It is no wonder that some time ago we heard that farmers in Saskatchewan had suggested that, if there was another war, they might not be quite so co-operative with the government as they had been in the last war. You cannot blame them for feeling that way. Time and again when I travelled in my constituency and when I was explaining to the farmers the British wheat agreement and other agreements and the fact that they were taking at that time less than they could have obtained if it had not been for government policy, I explained to them that the government had given a pledge that they would stabilize prices after the war, that they would support prices after the war. When I told them that,

many farmers said, "Do you think we can trust the government?" I said, "Yes; in this case I think you can; I think the government will stand by their promise". It is not a very happy situation in which I find myself when I am obliged to go back and face those farmers when they ask, "Do you still believe that the government are going to stand by their promise?" The government cannot expect me to defend them in that regard.
The government at the present time is showing little concern over the plight of the farmers. They apparently realize that the farmers are short of money. I think the government realizes that fact quite well and I think the Liberal members on the other side of the house realize it. But the strange thing is this. Instead of taking action to support the farmers, to help them, what do they do? They support the money lenders to help the farmers go further into debt. Practically all the legislation that is being brought down at the present time is designed not to support the farmers but to support the money lenders, to guarantee them against losses. The government bring down a farm loan bill to expand the amount of capital, to expand the amount of money that may be lent to farmers. It almost looks as though some people are rejoicing in the fact that at last the farmers are in a position where they will have to borrow more money.
It is true that during the war and in the early years after the war the farmers were able to pay off many of their mortgages. That fact was quoted time and again as proof of the fact that the farmers were doing well. But in the five years from 1948 to 1952, farm debt increased by 25 per cent. If farm debt increased by 25 per cent from 1948 to 1952, what has happened from 1952 to 1955? I am satisfied that farm debt has increased even more in that period of time. What has the government done to help that situation? It merely guarantees the banks. If the banks make loans to the farmers, the government will guarantee them against loss. Is it not about time the government started to guarantee the farmers instead of the financial institutions that are making these loans?
What is the situation with regard to the banks? After all, this is a bank bill. Would the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) suggest that the banks are in fairly bad shape today, that their reserves are disappearing and that their profits are falling? I think the Minister of Finance will agree that the banks are in an extremely healthy condition today and that they have substantial profits. Their reserves have been steadily expanding ever since the end of the war. Not only is that true of their
Grain
general reserves but in addition to their general reserves they have a secret reserve and they do not pay any income tax on- that inner reserve. I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that if the farmers were treated in that same way, were put in that preferred position, and were allowed to establish a secret reserve so that when their assets started to fall they could use that secret reserve to make up the losses of assets, and with no income tax charged them on that reserve, they probably would have been in a position today to meet their losses and to make up the loss of income resulting from the low prices today.
I do not know who drafted this bill. I should imagine that bankers drafted it because it is weighted so heavily in favour of the banks. The Minister of Finance shakes his head, but certainly I cannot imagine even bankers drafting a bill more advantageous to themselves than is this one. It is hedged with penalties from beginning to end. It is well to remember that the banks today are the only institutions in Canada that are in the preferred position of being able to monetize somebody else's wealth and then lend the proceeds to somebody at interest. That is a highly profitable business. But nobody else is in that happy position. I suggest that the farmers are in far greater need of assistance or support from the government than are the banks of this country. The government should attack vigorously the cause of the farmers* shortage of money which is, to a large extent, low prices.
At this point perhaps it is well to remind the house that this legislation is largely for the purpose of dealing with the question of wheat. What is the price of wheat today? The price of wheat today is just about half of parity price and by parity price I mean a price that bears a fair relationship to the price of other commodities. According to the dominion bureau of statistics, if the price of wheat today bore the same relationship to the price of other commodities as that which existed in the three base years used by the Agricultural Prices Support Act, namely 1943, 1944 and 1945, the price of wheat today would be $2.27 a bushel. What price are the farmers receiving? By the time you knock off freight charges, few farmers are getting more than about $1.25 a bushel under the initial payment.
I want to refer to the point that some hon. members have made. They have said, "You supported the bill at the resolution stage. We presume you are supporting the bill at this stage, in order to be consistent". May I say that we supported the resolution at the resolution stage after having bitterly criticized the measure. We voted in favour of the

Grain
resolution for the one purpose of allowing the government to bring in the bill. That is the purpose of the resolution. The bill is before us at the present time. Let me frankly admit there are many features of this bill, which we have now seen for the first time, which we heartily dislike. We dislike the section regarding penalties; we dislike the section regarding interest; and we dislike the section regarding storage, especially the section regarding storage. I cannot imagine why that section was ever put in the bill.
I am not permitted at this time to deal with any of those points, therefore I should like the minister-I see he is not in his seat; perhaps the Minister of Finance can give us assurance on this point-I should like the government to announce their intention to refer this bill to the standing committee on agriculture as soon as it receives second reading. Is the Minister of Finance prepared to say that when this bill receives second reading the government -will be prepared to refer it to the standing committee on agriculture so that it may call representatives from the various farm organizations to find out at first hand what these farm organizations really think about this bill?
We have heard hon. members from all sides of the house give different interpretations of how the farmers really feel about this matter. I suggest that instead of having to get this secondhand, we should get it firsthand. Let us refer this bill-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If my hon. friend would permit me to answer his question, the answer is no.

I thought that is what the government would say, and I am sorry to hear it, because it does not look as though the government really wants to get the advice of farm organizations on this matter. They do not really want to find out what the farm organizations think about this matter. It would be much easier for them to misquote the farm organizations at this time and try to give the impression that they are strongly in favour of loans at 5 per cent interest. I doubt very much whether there is any farmer in favour of that. They want advances.
If the government were prepared to send this bill to the agriculture committee upon second reading we would support the second reading; but if the government are not going to allow this bill to be sent to the agriculture committee, then they leave us no alternative but to support the C.C.F. amendment to refer the subject matter of the bill to the agriculture committee.
Another conversion.

It is not a question of conversion; it is a question of analysing the bill

before us and realizing that it does not meet the situation. At the resolution stage we had no bill; we had no details; we just had a resolution. We wanted to see the bill, and therefore we voted in favour of letting the bill be introduced in order to have the bill brought before the house. We do not like the bill; we do not like the way it deals with penalties, with interest and with the question of storage.
How are you going to vote on second reading?

Very definitely against second reading and in support of the amendment, in view of the minister's answer. We would have been prepared to support second reading provided that the government had been willing to allow the bill to go before the agriculture committee, but apparently the government does not want the farm organizations of this country to have the opportunity to tell the members of this parliament what they really feel about the bill. In other words, I smell a rat.
One hundred and seventy of them.
Mr. Speaker, I was not really making that allusion.
We will withdraw it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The bill is still odoriferous.

In dealing with the matter at the resolution stage the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that this measure was the same as the resolution submitted by the western conference to the government on October 11, 1955. I do not know how the minister could possibly come to that conclusion. He did not merely say it is the same, he said "exactly the same". Perhaps I had better quote his words. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) quoted the resolution and then the Minister of Trade and Commerce said: "That is exactly what we did". How he could possibly say that this bill is exactly what the western conference asked for I do not know. Just take the amount of the loan, $1,500. That is the limit of the loan. What was the limit asked for in the resolution of the western conference? They asked for an advance up to 50 per cent of the normal delivery. What would be the normal delivery? We might say 8 bushels to the acre. That was the amount of the quota last year, so we might say the normal delivery might be about 8 bushels to the acre. Just how would that work out, and what amount of loan would it provide? It all depends on the size of the farm, of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Has he any complaints from the big farmers about their inability to borrow money on their wheat?
I did not get the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I asked the hon. member whether he had heard any complaints from farmers farming a section or more of land about their inability to borrow from the banks without guarantees?

It all depends on the circumstances of the farmer. If a farmer is farming one or two sections and is buying that land on crop-share payments he is having one heck of a time to borrow money. It all depends on the circumstances; it all depends on the size of the farm. As I mentioned a while ago, it all depends on the financial standing of the farmer and how great reserves he has. That would determine whether or not the banks would lend him money and, of course, the character of the man. As I pointed out, there are many large farmers today who are in the unfortunate position of trying to pay for machinery and land, and they are having a great deal of difficulty. Take the size of the farm. Let us take what might be called an efficient unit. Professor Hope said that the most efficient unit to farm was two sections. An average man with the aid of a full line of machinery can handle two sections of fairly good land, but if you are farming gumbo land a section of land could use practically the same machinery as two sections of average land. Let us say that the amount of cultivated land would be 600 acres. Well, if a man had 600 acres, then 50 per cent of that, at 8 bushels to the acre, would amount to 2,400 bushels. The initial price of $1.25-that is about what the farmer would get-would give him $3,000. Therefore, taking that as the efficient unit of land, under the recommendation of the western farm unions, the amount of the advance would be about $3,000 instead of $1,500 provided in this bill.
So far as interest is concerned, while interest was not mentioned, the resolution referred to advances. There is no doubt that many of those representatives were talking about interest-free advances. However, some talked about a loan, really, rather than an advance, at a certain rate of interest, and apparently different rates of interest were mentioned. But I do not think anybody mentioned a rate of interest as high as 5 per cent. Three per cent was mentioned. In view of the fact
Grain
that the wheat board borrows money at 3 per cent, I cannot see why farmers-guaranteed by the government-have to pay 5 per cent.
The minister sometimes seems to think that 5 per cent is the normal rate of interest. There are many institutions borrowing money today at less than 5 per cent. Some of them are borrowing it at 3 per cent. When the loan is guaranteed by the government the banks certainly should be able to make loans at 3 per cent, even if for no other reason than to perform a public service. Therefore, the bill falls far short of the request made by the western conference, both in regard to the amount of the loan and the rate of interest.
The minister said that he cannot withdraw this bill; that if he withdrew it he would not be able to introduce another one this session. Of course, that all depends upon the bill. If he withdrew this bill, which is a loan bill, and introduced a bill to make payments to the farmers on wheat on the farm, he could no doubt introduce it because it would be another type of bill entirely. That is the type of bill the farmers want. They do not want loans, they want payments on the wheat in storage on the farms and if the government introduced a bill of that kind it would receive the wholehearted support of all the members on this side and I believe of all the farm organizations. If the government is not prepared to do that and is not prepared to refer this bill to the agricultural committee so the farm organizations may be called together to send representatives down here and tell us just what they think about the bill, the only alternative we have left is to support the C.C.F. amendment to send the subject matter of this bill to the agricultural committee and then we would have to vote against the bill as it is upon second reading.

This
is the first time that I have participated in this debate at its various stages. I do so because I regard the problem which confronts the wheat growers of western Canada as a problem that is national in its effects and as one in which the principle of government responsibility is directly involved.
The western wheat farmer has one marketing agency and one only. It is a government monopoly and the responsibility of the government in the face of the kind of situation that exists today in western Canada is therefore inescapable.
At this point, sir, may I say a word by way of review of the situation and concerning what it seems to me is the issue involved at this time. The government brought forward two resolutions both of which were

Crain
favourably reported by the committee of the whole. The first provided for the introduction of the bill that is now under debate, Bill No. 82, which was debated in committee for several days. The other resolution which was passed after only a cursory debate paved the way for the introduction of Bill No. 83.
The question has been raised about the position of parties in this house on these measures and in relation to the problem of the marketing of the wheat surplus in general. I wish to state briefly, and I trust succinctly, the position that we of the official opposition have taken in our approach to this problem.
First of all, we supported the resolution at that stage because, of course, as was stated then by our leader, we wished to see the measure advanced and no matter how far short it fell from our conception of what is needed in the way of policy and legislation to meet the problem we were not prepared to deny to the wheat farmer of the west anything that might offer even some slight advantage to him, so great is his need of cash at the present time.
When this bill was called for second reading yesterday we sought to express our views and our policy in regard to it in an amendment which, although it was ruled out of order, I just wish to mention in this connection. It reads:
That Bill No. 82 be not now read the second [DOT]ime, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introduction of legislation which will provide for cash payments on farm-stored grain.
Mr. Speaker ruled that amendment out of order, but the amendment stands as the expression of the view of this party as to the proper policy to be followed. In other words, it is a policy of cash advances on farm-stored grain. That is the position which this party has consistently taken in relation to this problem, and the gyrations and distortions which fell from the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) yesterday in regard to what is meant by cash advances will not change the fact or the policy.
The use of the expression "cash advances" has never signified the payment of interest. The hon. member yesterday brought in a weird suggestion that the use of the word "advance" connotes a loan on which interest will be paid. I do not think so weird a suggestion deserves even to have time spent upon it.
The position of this party has been made abundantly clear, for all who wish to understand it clearly, by the leader of this party when he said there was no thought whatever

of the imposition of interest on any payment that should be made to a farmer on account of farm-stored grain. That is the position this party has taken consistently. It is the position this party has taken for years in relation to this whole subject. It was enunciated by my leader in this house in debate in December 1952, and that was not the first time it had been put forward. Consistently we have advocated the policy of cash advances against farm-stored grain and that is still our policy.

speechtext:
