He has continued at some length along tiffs line and I am just asking myself whether he is in order in doing so. May I draw his attention to citation 245, which reads in part as follows:
It is a wholesome restraint upon members that they cannot revive a debate already concluded . . .
There was some discussion of this matter yesterday and the amendment was ruled out of order. Therefore I should think that the hon. member should refrain from reviving that part of the debate.

Sir, I was not discussing the amendment but I was discussing the policy, and the policy is necessarily relevant to the debate on second reading of this bill because it is the proper alternative to the kind of policy that is embodied in the bill. The fact that the amendment was ruled out of order does not preclude a proper discussion of policy in relation to the problem that this bill seeks-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Which policy has already been rejected by the house.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, quite.
No sir, the policy has not been rejected by the house. The amendment was ruled out of order and the minister went on yesterday after that at page 1177-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. One of the
reasons, as I understand it, that Mr. Speaker ruled the amendment out of order was that the house expressed its opinion on that very point on a previous amendment and therefore I do not see that the hon. gentleman is on sound ground.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to prolong that part of my remarks, but I do wish to state that at page 1177 of yesterday's Hansard, after this matter had)

been dealt with by Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Trade and Commerce took it upon himself to say:
We all know that the Conservative party has no policy.
That is right.

I am stating that the policy of the Conservative party has been and is the policy of cash advances on farm-stored grain. We sought to give expression to that policy in the amendment yesterday. The amendment was ruled out of order, and 1 regret that the house did not have an opportunity to deal specifically with that policy.
On the other hand, what does the bill provide for? It proposes to empower the government to guarantee loans up to $1,500 in each case made by banks to farmers as against grain, such loans to bear interest at the rate of 5 per cent. The minister says that since the banks embarked upon these loans several months ago on the strength of a promise by the government to ask parliament to pass legislation such as we understand to be embodied in Bill 82, about 8,000 loans have been made. We are told that this bill to provide for government guarantees on individual loans and the associated measure to provide for payment by the government of storage charges on wheat are all the government proposes to do. This is the sum total of the government's legislative program in answer to this problem.
What then is the principle of this bill? On the resolution stage we said, and we say it now with emphasis, that we deplore the utter inadequacy of the government's program to meet the need. An inadequacy so patent has been accompanied on the part of the government by taunts and expressions of contempt for parliament; the use by the Minister of Trade and Commerce of such expressions as "bunkum" applied to serious arguments put forward by opposition members who spoke with responsibility and a knowledge of the feelings of western Canada.
It is quite obvious that the western wheat farmer sought justice. He did not come on bended knee. What he sought was a proper loaf; but, as has been said on behalf of this party from the outset, it is quite clear that this measure is not even half a loaf. In relation to the need of the kind of policy I have described, it is at best not more than a crust.
There are times when a vote in the house on an issue when taken alone and apart from statements which precede it is not an adequate expression of the feelings of a party on that issue. We of the official opposition desire to express our indignation at the utter inadequacy of this measure to meet the need. At the same time we have no wish, in the
Grain
face of the patent inadequacy of the government's program, to deny to the necessitous wheat farmers of western Canada even the paltry crust which this measure offers to 8,000 of them. We have considered ourselves as being under an obligation as a party to make every determined effort to obtain for the western wheat farmers something adequate, something much better than this inadequate measure. If a proper policy of cash advances, such as has been advocated, were adopted it would be a simple matter to take care of the 8,000 loans which have been made by the banks in western Canada in anticipation of the enactment of such a bill as this. The farmers would then be in position to repay those loans to the banks out of the cash advances.
Not having had an opportunity to vote upon our amendment I come now to the amendment introduced yesterday by the C.C.F. It has already been made clear that it is our purpose to support that amendment and I wish to give one or two reasons for our views in that regard. The amendment is in these terms:
That Bill No. 82 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization.
From the Social Credit party the house heard today a proposal that in the event of the bill receiving second reading the government should at that stage permit the bill to be sent to the committee on agriculture and colonization so that representations could be heard from the farm organizations of western Canada. One would have thought that that was a reasonable, indeed a modest proposal; but this arrogant government has rejected that proposal out of hand. It had hardly left the lips of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), as government leader, rose and rejected it out of hand. So we are then faced with the situation where the government will have nothing to do with any suggestion that this measure go to a committee, whether before second reading or after.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, no, it is going to the committee of the whole.

Why does the minister
quibble? Who does he think is going to yield to nonsense of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not nonsense.

Of course it will go to the committee of the whole. Every measure goes to the committee of the whole, but the whole purpose of referring a measure of this kind to a select standing committee is to provide opportunity for intimate discussion and the

Grain
hearing of representations by those whose representations in connection with the matter this government ought to welcome. But they do not wish even the farm organizations of western Canada to be heard here on Parliament Hill. It is much better for their purposes that they go forward garbling what has been said elsewhere on behalf of the farm organizations in western Canada.
There have been statements made in the course of this debate as to the position of the farm organizations. There have been contradictory statements by the minister as to what the farm organizations had conveyed to the government. Surely in the face of this situation the fair way of handling it would be to invite those organizations to speak with authority before a select standing committee of the house.
It was not always so. The government when faced with such a situation has not always taken upon itself to reject such a proposal out of hand. Not always when a proposal was made by the opposition that the subject matter of a bill be referred to one of the select standing committees for consideration has the government risen in its wrath and said that it would kill the bill.
If there were on the part of the government a sincere desire to understand the problems of the west and to offer effective measures within the scope of parliamentary responsibility to meet the need of western Canada, then the government would surely welcome a proposal that would place this matter before a committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I might say that representatives of the most powerful agricultural organization in western Canada were here not later than yesterday to meet the government and in the course of an hour and a half did not once mention the subject matter of this bill.
I wonder if they were given a chance.
That is pretty complete proof that they did not like it very well or they would not have mentioned it.

It would indeed be interesting if the government would permit such an opportunity to be shared with a select standing committee of the house where we could elicit the facts.
As I have said, the government did not always take this attitude. There was a time when the government did not say that the adoption of an amendment like the one now under discussion would kill the bill and therefore it must not be entertained. On May 14, 1946, there was before the house-I refer to this as a precedent in relation to

proper procedure in connection with this matter-Bill No. 54, to amend the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, 1942. That was a government measure and the then minister of labour, the late Humphrey Mitchell, moved the second reading. An extended discussion followed and strong criticism was levelled at the bill by the opposition. But, if you please, not only did the government accept an amendment that the bill should not be read a second time but that its subject matter be referred to a committee of the house, but a minister offered that amendment. At page 1533 of Hansard of May 14, 1946, it will be found that at the conclusion of the debate on the second reading of that bill Hon. Ian A. Mackenzie proposed the following amendment to what was a government bill:
That the bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the select committee on veterans affairs with instructions that they shall consider the same and report thereon to the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What happened then?
It went to the committee, and the committee made its report and recommendations to the house. The house dealt with the bill in the light of the recommendations of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A new bill.
Yes. What was wrong with that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not arguing; I am merely telling you.

The result was a very much improved bill, but apparently the government does not want an improved bill in this case. There was no difference in principle between the situation that then confronted the house on May 14, 1946, and the one that confronts the house today, February 15, 1956. There was no difference in principle, but there was this difference in fact. The government then had a narrow majority and it was not dominated by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce. Today the government has a swollen, silent, supine majority, and the government is dominated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That is the difference.
As I understand it, the purpose of the amendment that is now under debate is to give an effective opportunity for reviewing the problem and trying to bring forward some more effective measure to deal with it, and at least trying to clear up all the contradictions as to the attitudes of those principally concerned as expressed through the farm organizations.
Is there a problem confronting the wheat farmer of western Canada, and if so, is it

a problem that is national in its effects and dangers? I say, "yes". To listen to the government talk, and particularly the familiar optimistic tones of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, one would just think there is no problem at all. On January 16 of this year the Minister of Trade and Commerce, after making some sarcastic references to the opposition, said:
Shortages are wonderful, to be solved by simply denying their existence.
What is the government's attitude here? If I might paraphrase the remarks of the minister, it would be this: problems arising out of surpluses are wonderful, to be solved by the government by simply denying their existence. So far as the government is concerned, everything is perfect. Wheat is moving; sales are running up; prices are good; there is no question of unused farm storage. Everything is perfect, nothing is wrong, and a surplus is a good thing. That seems to be the government's position. The government, having no solution to this problem, is content to deny the existence of the problem. Baron Munchausen at his best could not have done better.
He never met the minister.

As to the worth of the minister's statements, it would be well for us to recall this glowing statement made by the minister in this house on February 18, 1955- this is almost the anniversary of these remarks he made in the house at that time- as recorded on page 1312 of Hansard:
However, as I say, our sales are very good. I can assure hon. members, I think with certainty, that before the crop year ends on July 31 any producer who has grain of any kind that he wishes to market will have had an opportunity of marketing it. The suggestion of storage on the farm, I feel, is one that will not help very much, considering the short period that should ensue between now and the day the wheat grower will be able to market all the grain he has to market.
Again, as recorded on page 1313, he said:
We will have a substantial carryover of wheat, but that wheat will all be in public storage. Storage on the farm will no longer be a problem to western Canada.
What a travesty of the facts! What a prophecy! When we hear the minister indulging in his prophecies again, the easy optimism, the denial of the existence of the problem, I ask the house to weigh the worth of the minister's statements of that kind against the equally worthless statements that he was asking this house to accept one year ago.
It is getting worse all the time.

The problem is one of lack of cash income to the western farmer, arising
Grain
from the failure of this monopolistic government agency to market his grain. The government refuses to deal with the situation in a way that would meet the needs.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I thought you invented the monopoly.

We have demonstrated that not only does the government not wish a better measure, but they do not wish to treat parliament as parliament ought to be treated in these matters. What is the hallmark of a free parliament? It seems to me there are two tests. The first is that parliament, by its very name, is a place to talk. That is the democratic method. No matter how the talk may try the patience of some, it has still been proven in the long run, over the long years and centuries of testing, to be the best method. We have tried to persuade by the method of talking.
That is not the method that was practised in Hitlerite Germany. That is not the method of Russia; there, when the masters of the Kremlin choose to address the presidium, they simply call the presidium together and make their statements. It is a sort of counterpart, I suppose, of the speech from the throne, a review of the things the government has done, and the assembled legislators hear these declarations. There are perhaps two or three speeches by members selected for the purpose. The members simply hold up their hands to pass whatever is required by way of legislation, and then they go home.
The other hallmark of a free parliament is the right to criticize, and criticize freely. Another hon. member of this house, the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) and I were two of a group of half a dozen Canadians who in the fall of 1948 visited Greece and were received in the Greek assembly during the course of a debate. The debate was interrupted for the purpose of having tributes paid to Canada, particularly in the light of what Canada had done through the Red Cross and Canadian aid to Greece through the allied war relief fund. I recall how heated was the debate before we came in, and with what heat an opposition member was criticizing the government.
When I came back home and was addressing a meeting at a Canadian university and relating this incident, which happened at a time when the communists were seeking to overrun Greece and there was great distress, warfare and bloodshed in that country, a communist stood up at the back of the hall and asked, "How can you pretend that the Greek parliament is a free parliament?" My answer to him was this: "The test of a free parliament is the right to criticize, and I heard pungent criticism of the government

Grain
being offered in that house by an opposition member." That to me was proof enough of the existence of freedom in the Greek parliament.
So I say there are two hallmarks of a free parliament. One is talk; it is a place to talk. The other is the right to criticize freely. Here in this debate we have had further, and indeed unnecessary, proofs of the fact that this government does not want a free parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, now, just a moment.
The government regulates the business that comes before the house-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege. Nothing whatever that has ever been said in my time in this house would justify a remark like that.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A free parliament is something that all of us seek to uphold and maintain, and I suggest that hon. members are not in order to say otherwise.
Sir, with-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I must agree with the minister on this point of order. I am sure that on reflection, the hon. member for Eglinton will also agree and will revise his remarks accordingly. While I am on my feet, may I also remind the hon. member for Eglinton that for some time he has been directing his remarks to what I might call a philosophic discussion of parliament. We are actually dealing with the second reading of a bill dealing with a very particular subject.
I must ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the principle of the bill.
That is just what I am proposing to do. You will see the relevance of these remarks. This government has sought to stifle debate on this measure.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I indicated that the minister's point of order was well taken, and I thought the hon. member for Eglinton would commence his remarks by revising his previous remark in that connection.
I am saying, Mr. Speaker, that this government has sought to stifle debate on this measure.
At no time.

Let me get on with my
evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have no objection to my hon. friend making a statement of opinion of that kind, but the question of whether or not one

is attempting to stifle parliament is a different matter. This matter of opinion can be argued in debate between us, but saying we are seeking to change a free parliament is a different matter.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, may I ask you whether or not you, at the request of the minister, are not seeking to stifle opinion. This is a question of opinion, and you are seeking to stifle it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope the hon. member for Greenwood is not attempting to suggest that the Minister of Finance is putting words in my mouth. That implication will not be allowed to remain. I did agree that the point of order raised by the minister was well taken when the hon. member for Eglinton had said that the government was attempting to stifle a free parliament, or words to that effect; I will get the exact words in Hansard tomorrow. That was a statement of fact, and I think that implication should be withdrawn by the hon. member.

If it will meet the situation, sir, I will say that in my opinion this government is trying to stifle a free parliament. They have tried to stifle debate on this measure. It started on January 27, the very first day of the debate, when the minister, in the course of his remarks, tried to frighten members of this house into refraining from making remarks critical of government policy. He proceeded to say there was no occasion for a prolonged debate on this measure. We had a short day on Friday, January 27 and a short day on Friday, February 3. Wednesday, February 8 was a half day, and at that time the minister rose and made some very inaccurate remarks. His patience was exhausted, because he has no patience for debate and no patience for criticism. He said then, when this measure had been debated for only part of two days, that we had been a long time on this debate.
Then he went on to say that it seemed to him no more repetitive speeches were needed, and that some members of the opposition had spoken twice while one was about to speak for the third time. It was proven that was not a fact, and no member of the group to which he referred had spoken more than once. Then he said there was no need for debate on the principle of this bill. Is that not an attempt to stifle parliament? He said he was willing to drop the measure until June and charged that those who were critical of the government's policy were simply seeking to block and obstruct. Yesterday we had the minister making the extraordinary statement in this house that, after all, he is too busy to sit in the house and listen to a debate of

this kind. At page 1177 of Hansard for February 14, 1956, the minister said:
I do not know why you have to again listen to the speeches we have just heard. We have already heard the same men making the same speeches.
Then he goes on:
I really begrudge the time. Her Majesty pays me tor doing something useful and I do not think I am earning my pay when I have to sit here in the house and listen to the kind of blather we have been having on this particular bill.
Oh, oh.

Is that the speech of a sincere believer in democracy? I say that kind of speech would better belong to the other kind of assembly to which I referred in other countries rather than in a free parliament. Neither that attitude nor that kind of speech has any place in a free parliament. The attitude exposed is not the attitude of anyone who has any knowledge of or sympathy with the proper functions of a free parliament. When the hon. member for Rosthern was speaking the minister interrupted him to say that he would soon be turning this discussion into a debate, and naturally he does not want a debate.
So we are left with this situation. First, there has been in fact no obstruction. The charge the minister has made in that respect is entirely lacking in truth. Second, the minister has been very angry. He objects to listening to criticism. He does not want debate. He does not want reply to the wild accusations he has made.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What are you reading from?

He just does not belong in a free parliament with an approach like that. He just does not feel at home and therefore it is natural he should not wish to sit here; he would prefer to spend his time outside. If it is such a bother to him to spend his time in parliament, there is nothing to prevent him from leaving this parliament. Third, he has indulged in threats to the members to frighten them into silence. He threatened dissolution yesterday; that was intended to frighten Liberal members of this house. I am sure it had no effect on anybody else. These threats make a mockery of parliamentary process.
Fourth, I say the Liberals in this house are on trial. If you believe in a free parliament, then for pity's sake express yourself and do not sit in this house like mummies. Do not allow the minister to tell you, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce told you on January 18, that from now on you must toe the party line. When members of a free parliament are told by one of the ministers that from now on they must toe the party
Grain
line I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that it puts every Liberal member in this house on trial. If he toes the line, then of course he will be a good boy. If he wishes to preserve a free parliament, then let him assert his independence and refuse to be told how to think about this great national problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: On a point of order, what is all this harangue about? It does not have anything to do with this bill or this amendment.

It has a great deal to do with the supine and submissive Liberals in this house in relation to this measure and in the face of the needs of western Canada that are not being met by this inadequate measure.

may say that I have no wish to hold up this debate, but I want to take two or three minutes to deal with some of the remarkable points raised by members of Her Majesty's official opposition. In the amusing talk we heard last night from the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), which I think certainly put the house in good humour, there was one serious point which even in my humble capacity I would not like to allow to go unchallenged. The hon. member suggested that there was something wrong in this government holding out a helping hand to Britain in a time of great need when she stood entirely alone against the whole forces of fascism in Europe, and when this country held out a helping hand by giving Britain a long-guaranteed supply of wheat at a fair price.
There was another remarkable point, Mr. Speaker, raised by-

On a point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I cannot allow the hon. member's statement to pass because at no time in this house, during wartime or peacetime, have I ever suggested we should not give a helping hand to Britain. On different occasions I have urged that we give them more. It was in relation to the British agreement deal that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made that I was speaking, and to twist it the way the hon. member has is to misinterpret it in unfairness to me.

If I have misinterpreted the hon. member, I am sorry, but when I read his remarks in Hansard he was objecting to the fact that we sold Britain a supply of wheat at much less than world prices, and especially to selling Britain wheat for about a dollar a bushel less than otherwise she would have had to pay.
I now want to deal with the other rather remarkable point made by my good and genial

Grain
friend the hon. member tor Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) who, I note, has just .stepped behind the curtain, when he suggests the Minister of Trade and Commerce should follow the example of the great Conservative leader Disraeli in the year 1867 and when he found there was opposition to a certain resolution which he proposed, he should withdraw the resolution gracefully. I have been looking up the book to which the hon. gentleman referred. Jennings' "Parliamentary Reform", page 243, gives the incident to which my hon. friend refers. The incident would certainly interest the old professor of history, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). It was when the great Conservative leader was trying to put through his reform bill to give the franchise to more of the voters of Britain and to abolish the rotten borough principle. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the members of Her Majesty's opposition are certainly on extremely weak ground-
This has nothing to do with the bill.

-when they have to thresh over old straw not only once but twice and three times, and when they go all the way back to Disraeli and then, by implication at least, criticize that great Conservative leader for having tried to put through the second reform bill.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, by trying to hold up the passage of this bill and by making the same speeches not once but twice, three times, four times, five times and six times, not only reviving the debate on the speech from the throne but debate at the various stages of this bill, members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition are doing exactly the same thing today to which they violently objected when the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested last week that we might be obliged to postpone this bill. By suggesting that this bill should be sent to the committee on agriculture and colonization they are in fact saying that the western farmers are in no hurry for cash advances of any kind and can afford to wait for months and months.
That is twisting the record.
You had better get back to family allowances.

Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I might remind him that three months have passed since the Minister of Trade and Commerce made his announcement. If parliament has been able to wait for three months, I see no reason *why we should not wait long enough to act

on the suggestion made by my colleague the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Johnson). The amendment before us is that Bill 82 be not now read the second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is old enough and has been here long enough to know that if he will only say the word, this reasonable request can be granted. When the minister was leading the house some years ago I had the honour of presenting an amendment asking that the question of milk subsidies be reconsidered, and the minister turned around and suggested there should be a free vote on that subject. There was such a vote and the amendment carried, and the government was not defeated. I suggest that all that needs to be done now is for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to say that this is a question that deserves the impartial consideration of all members of the house and that there will be a free vote.
The fate of the government will not depend on the outcome of that vote. If a majority is of the opinion that this bill should not now be read the second time but that the subject matter should be referred to the standing committee so that witnesses can be called, in the light of the discussion and the decision, the government can then decide whether or not it wishes to bring in additional legislation.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has used a good deal of material that I planned on using. I want to thank him for that.
Do it again.
Mr. Speaker, I resent the suggestion of filibuster and delay.
That is what you are doing.

If there is anyone on the government side of the house who feels that this matter is being delayed, all you have to do is bring in a motion of closure and with your government majority the motion will carry.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is what you want.

When you were in the chair yesterday afternoon, Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) was speaking, you were surprised-as was I-to have the Minister of Trade and Commerce say this, as reported at page 1161 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, are we having a debate on second reading or-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I did not hear the point of order raised by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
On second reading I do not think that this speech should be allowed to degenerate into a debate.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that one who is getting so old and tired as to make that sort of interjection in this sort of debate must be causing a good deal of embarrassment to his younger colleagues-
Don't worry about that.

-when he suggests later on, as reported at page 1177 of Hansard:
I do not know why we have to again listen to the speeches we have just heard.
Mr. Speaker, you are following closely what is being said, as are other members and I am sure that if anyone on the opposition side was attempting to make a speech that had already been made since that controversial subject arose, you would have been quick to draw attention to the fact that at page so and so of Hansard the speech was to be found. But these speeches are not speeches which have been given. The minister said:
I have other things to do. I really begrudge the time. Her Majesty pays me for doing something useful and I do not think I am earning my pay when I have to sit here in the house and listen to the kind of blather we have been having on this particular bill.
Who said that?
Those are the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
It could not be anybody else.
Read it again.

In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, those words are a reflection on parliament. As the hon. member for Eglinton has suggested, if the minister is too busy or too tired to hear what is being said on this particular subject, let him do what he suggested he would like to do. Let him go away or do whatever he likes.
Go Ashing.
Yes; go fishing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If he does not think he is earning his pay, he does not need to take it.

When the minister spoke on this subject some little time ago he cited the case of the meeting he attended when there was someone who was critical, I presume, of government policy on agriculture. After the meeting was over the gentleman who was so vocal gave the Minister of Trade and Commerce a lift and the conversation is alleged to have run something like this: "After all, conditions are not as tough as I indicated". The minister said, "This is a nice car you are
Grain
driving." "Of course; it is a new car and I like it." The farmer said, "It has been the goal of my lifetime to be in a position where I was free of debt, with a crop in the bins and was sitting pretty; and I am happy to be in that position now". Then the minister concluded by saying, "That is the position of the western farmer".
A scandalous remark.

After hearing him, Mr. Speaker, I could not let the resolution pass without challenging the fairness of that sort of statement. I was reminded of the report of a speech which his colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) delivered in New York.
We heard it.

No, you did not hear this speech; I did not have it. This is what the Minister of Finance said on November 2 last when he was speaking as the guest of the Canadian Club in New York. I suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce should read this speech; it is excellent. After giving a review of the Canadian scene, the Minister of Finance had this to say:
The wheat problem, as it exists today is not just a product of the temporary generosity of nature. The roots of the problem go much deeper than this. They lie in the national policies of a number of countries. Basically, the large stocks of wheat have arisen because of world acreage expansion. This acreage expansion has been the result of national policies of subsidies and tariff protection. The consequence of acreage expansion has been higher production. The estimated production for 1955 is not far short of 71 billion bushels compared with about 6 billion bushels for the average of 1935 to 1939.
United States wheat production has increased proportionately over pre-war figures considerably more than world production; and the building up of very substantial unsold surplus has resulted. The ways and means by which the United States reduces these surpluses is of serious, indeed, vital interest to us.
In Canada we have a central selling agency for wheat, the Canadian wheat board, but we do not subsidize the wheat producer. The wheat grower in Canada receives an initial price on delivery and eventually a final payment which represents the net price received by the wheat board after meeting all costs of storing, handling, transporting and selling the crop.
The Canadian wheat producer is fully prepared to compete on equal terms in the world wheat market. He has confidence in the quality of his product and his technical efficiency in producing it. However, it is quite another thing to compete with wheat grown in other countries where it is heavily protected by either high tariffs or high subsidies, or both. The problem of the Canadian wheat producer will only be solved with the removal of these high artificial barriers which now restrict, directly and indirectly, our access to the world wheat market. But I can only repeat-wheat production is the principal source of cash income of the great majority of our western

Grain
farmers and we, as a government, are bound to be greatly influenced by anything so vital to them and to our national economy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Am I expected to applaud?

No, but I would expect the minister's colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to do him the courtesy of at least reading this speech and learning of the views the Minister of Finance made known at the meeting in New York city when he was invited to address the Canadian Club. If this matter was of such importance, and it was, for the Minister of Finance, in the middle of a very interesting and accurate review of the whole Canadian economy, to take time to point it up, then I suggest, that the two eldest and senior members of the cabinet, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture, are doing a great disservice to their colleagues, to parliament, and to the people of Canada in suggesting that there is no problem; that it is a situation that is not to be worried about.
When speaking at another place the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
The Prime Minister lays down the party line. Once that line is laid down, I don't care whether you are a member of the House of Commons or the Senate, that line should be adhered to. We stand or fall together.
What has that to do with this debate?
I suggest there is an amendment before the house, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that if the backbenchers cannot support it the government will fall.
Who said so?

The minister has said it is a want of confidence motion. The Minister of Agriculture said:
When the majority of the Liberal party agrees that a thing should be done I am going to work to see that it is done.
Whether it is right or wrong, so long as it is the party line. Not so Senator Power-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Watch your desk.

Senator Power said:
It has not been many generations since men struggled to destroy forever the doctrine of the divine right of kings.
Cherishing these traditions and honouring those proponents of a free parliament I cannot bring myself to believe-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
have, perhaps incorrectly, allowed references to pronouncements by the minister who sponsors the bill and by the minister responsible for the Department of Agriculture because they might conceivably have some bearing upon the questions before us. But I must

express the definite opinion that expressions of political philosophy by someone in another place, not dealing with the question of guaranteed bank loans to farmers, is not in order in the present debate.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. But, as the Minister of Finance pointed out so correctly in New York city, the Canadian farmer cannot compete in the world with producers in other countries who are subsidized or where there are tariffs. In Chile the farmers receive the equivalent of $4.50 a bushel; Switzerland, $4.19; Norway, $3.43; Sweden, $2.35; Argentina, $2.72; and the United States, $2.24. So long as wheat is coming from countries that have these large subsidies, while we are trying to compete with wheat without any assistance, we shall be in a hopeless position.
Last night the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. White) spoke, and I was glad to have him take part in the debate. I am aware of the fact that those of us from the wheat-producing area have taken considerable time of parliament this session.
Not nearly enough.

I am sure in our remarks we have not suggested that there are no problems in other parts of Canada. I am sure that the hon. member for Waterloo South is a reasonable person and that on reflection he will not support what he said last night, which is as follows, as reported at page 1183 of Hansard:
The more I listen to the C.C.F. representatives from western Canada the more I am convinced that they are not concerned with the welfare of the western wheat farmers as much as they are with political expediency.
Well, I think that was not a useful contribution to make to this debate. The Toronto Star, which supports the present government very faithfully, considered this question important enough to send one of their ablest reporters, Robert Nielson, to Saskatchewan to find out from the grass roots, if there is a problem, and Mr. Nielson has an article in the last issue of the Kelvington Radio that just reached me. He has had interviews with farmers on their farms. On the train coming out from Saskatoon he met a farmer by the name of Mr. Rediger who told him about the conditions on his farm. He called on several farmers who gave figures with regard to their expenses and incomes for the year.
Part of the report reads:
Rediger broached a theme that was to be stated, politely but firmly, by nearly every westerner I talked with. He contrasted the position of the prairie farmer at the mercy of the world market for his income, with the happy state of workers and managers in eastern industry, sheltered by tariffs (which jack up the farmers' living and operating expense).

The report mentioned a hardware store in the town of Wadena, with a stock of $40,000 to $50,000, I would say. The hardware merchant said that one day the previous week he had sold 10 cents worth of goods'.

Here is a situation the Toronto Star considers a matter of national concern and on which it sends one of its top reporters to Saskatchewan by aeroplane. He sees the people in their farm homes and in town. The secretaries of the municipalities point out that without exception every municipality in my constituency has reported tax arrears are away up from a year ago.
As Mr. Rediger pointed out, the thing which annoys the farm people is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce can correctly say that business is booming. International Nickel in 1954 had a net profit after taxes of $65 million; Imperial Oil, $49 million; Distillers Corporation, $35 million; Aluminium Limited, $33 million; Bell Telephone, $28 million. Every other sector of our economy is prosperous; yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce refuses to consider his own statistical information.
The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) took part in the debate. I am sorry that an hon. member from an industrial riding should have tried to create the impression that the farmers in Saskatchewan are in high income tax brackets, and that when the war was on they purchased victory bonds as soon as they were issued while industrial workers were unable to do so.
I am happy to note that in a publication of the bureau of statistics which came to me it was pointed out that labour income from January to October of last year indicated an increase of 7 per cent. Wages were up 7 per cent; they reached an all-time high, and that is as it should be. I think if the labourer receives a good pay cheque he is going to be able to buy more food, and food of better quality.
I might say that the attitude of the hon. member for Kootenay East, who said in effect that we are misrepresenting the plight of the farmer and that after all the farmer is getting more than he deserves, is different from the attitude presented by most industrial organizations. It is typical of the trade union

Grain
movement on the whole to recognize that this is one of the problems in Canada, that farm people are not getting their fair share of the national income. Some bon. members have gone into the farming areas and suggested that the farmer's trouble is caused by the fact that the industrial worker is getting such high wages.
In the United States the U.A.W. recently made a study when steel prices went up in that country. In a circular issued by the U.A.W. in Washington I note on page 9 it is pointed out that the corporation profits before taxes went up 65 per cent and corporation profits after taxes went up 41 per cent; dividends paid by corporations were up 73 per cent but the farmers' net income was down 28 per cent.
The U.A.W. realize that when this happens they cannot sell automobiles and farmers cannot buy farm machinery. They point out that when the price of steel went up $7.50 a ton that year-
The price of what?

When the price of steel went up. This sort of increase creates some resentment for labour. The automobile workers had an increase of 21 cents an hour, and this increase would have warranted an increase in G.M. labour costs to the extent of $49 million. Instead of increasing by $49 million, they increased by $570 million. In the farm implement industry it should be pointed out that when Deere and Company gave an extra dollar to their workers, they collected $1.96 from their customers, and when the Oliver Corporation gave an extra dollar they charged $2.05. I am sure that the hon. member for Mackenzie will agree with me that the relationship between wage increases and the cost to the consumer of manufactured goods is so far from the question as to whether or not the particular bill should be referred to the committee on agriculture that it cannot be regarded as being in order in this debate.

But I think I am fully entitled to ask the hon. member to bring his argument much closer to the subject matter before us than he has been doing during the last four or five minutes.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your point and it is very well taken, but unfortunately government members who 
have taken part in this debate, particularly the hon. member for Waterloo South, who was permitted to discuss butter last night during this debate, have been allowed to wander. If hon. members on the other side are to be permitted to discuss everything under the sun, then I think hon. members on this side should be able to do likewise.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: am going to take it upon myself this time to interrupt the hon. gentleman and indicate that I interrupted the hon. member for Waterloo South yesterday of my own volition.

I shall not pursue that matter any further, as I want to leave some time in which to say something about the Minister of Agriculture. The minister should know better than to come to parliament and present the proposition that the farmers have never been as prosperous. The minister would be quite right in saying that the farmers of Canada are much better off than the farmers of India, the farmers of Pakistan or the farmers of a great many other countries, but that is not the point. The farmers of Canada are receiving a diminishing share of the national income as their costs are going up.
No one knows this better than the Minister of Agriculture. The other day he started to give us some figures on farm net income, and pointed out that the net income picture was pretty serious in the prairie provinces, but that taking a five-year period the situation was quite different.
On checking the Parliamentary Guide I find that the Minister of Agriculture was first elected to represent the people in 1914, 42 years ago. No wonder he is getting old and tired. I find that 34 years ago he was given cabinet responsibility, and that for the last 34 years he has been either a cabinet minister or the leader of an opposition. With that sort of record he should be in a position to speak with some authority over a long period. But when he suggests that the farmers in the west are in a very favourable position, or if they are not it is their own fault, he is doing a great disservice. The Minister of Agriculture gets the equivalent of $500 every Saturday night.
He does not have to borrow.

He does not have to worry about a bank loan. If farming is as prosperous as he has indicated he should be able to make enough on his farm to pay his income tax. Any farmer who could count on $500 a week would not be worrying about a bank loan. I think the figures I have given with reference to arrears of taxes in northeastern Saskatchewan suggest that there are

very few people who have the good fortune the Minister of Agriculture has had in having such good health and a guaranteed income over such a long period. He is performing no service for agriculture by making that sort of suggestion.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has just handed me a little circular which I presume all hon. members have received, which indicates that the C.C.F. members here are backed by a considerable claque of wheat pool interests. Claque is defined as being a body of ap-plauders, or hired applause. It points out that fortunately the government is not going to yield to our pressure and that the Canadian government has rightly refused to lick the boots of pressure groups whose main objective is to soak the Canadian taxpayer.
Before I conclude may I say that I wish the backbenchers would reconsider this matter and decide whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce was speaking for them when he suggested that they follow the party line. I should like to extend an invitation to the committee to meet in northeastern Saskatchewan. The accommodation there may not be quite as good as at the Chateau or in this building, but the best accommodation available in my constituency would be forthcoming for a meeting of a special committee to hear witnesses.
I think it is significant that the Minister of Justice has not made the same sort of mistake as was made by his colleagues, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture. I would be surprised if the Minister of Justice suggested at his Minnedosa meeting that the farmers of Canada are as prosperous as the Minister of Trade and Commerce said they were or as his colleague the Minister of Agriculture indicated. I hope serious consideration will be given to having this matter referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization in order to give the delegation which met the cabinet yesterday a chance to put their cards on the table and tell all Canada that we are wrong, that the farmers they represent are enjoying an era of prosperity seldom experienced in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I did not speak during the resolution stage nor on the second reading, and I perhaps should not be speaking now as the position of the Social Credit group has been placed on the record more than once, but I rise to speak because of one word emphatically expressed by the Minister of Finance, when he said "no". I listened to the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) with great interest as I always do. We regard him as one of our

exceptionally expert men when it comes to' matters of finance and trade and agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I agree wholly with that; do not dissociate me from that.

I was not connecting the "no" with what I am saying now. I listened to the hon. member's speech, and as usual it was sensible, it was most reasonable, it was logical and, as all his speeches are, it was filled with sound judgment. His speeches are very seldom destructive, and in this instance he did not tear down anything. The speech he made this afternoon, I thought, was exceptionally constructive. His request was most reasonable. He stood here as a sort of peacemaker between the government, which is asking the confidence of this house, and a number of members on the opposition side who do not wish to vote confidence on this bill.
The suggestion he made was that we in this group should vote confidence on second reading, provided the government were a little more reasonable. He did not even ask the government to change its position. All he wanted was that the government would be more reasonable and on its own initiative send the bill to the committee without a vote on the amendment. It is going to be voted upon, but as far as our group are concerned we would vote against the amendment if the minister would send the bill on second reading to the committee on agriculture and colonization. But the minister interrupted my hon. friend and said, "The answer is no." It was a very emphatic no, and we all know that no meant no. Sometimes I wonder whether the government knows exactly its constitutional position.
No.

I have my ideas about it. The government assumes it was elected to bring some bills down. The government of this country is never elected. It is members of parliament who are elected, and they as individuals were elected by their constituents. Of course if they represent the party with the biggest majority, their leader is asked to form a government, and able men of the party are called in to form that government. But they assume that they speak for parliament. I might ask boldly, "Who do they think they are? Do they think they represent the people?"
The fact of the matter is that their actions would indicate that they have no regard for the people's wishes. The proposal that was made by the hon. member for Acadia on behalf of his group was a very reasonable one: "The bill is not all we want, but we

Grain
will vote for it, if he will send it to the committee on second reading, so that representatives can come and express their views." There are people representing various organizations who could appear before the committee and make their views known.
Now, let me ask what are standing committees for if they are not to look into the details of bills and hear representations from groups of interested people in this country?
Members of parliament are elected to represent the people.
I recognize that, but what my hon. friend over here is saying is that therefore we do not need any standing committee.
No, he was careful not to say that. He was trying to put you right on law.
He said it by inference. We have our standing committees for a purpose. Those standing committees are to hear representations on various bills and other matters.
No, they are not. They are to consider matters which are referred to them. That is their function.

I did not say anything different from that. That is what we are asking. We are asking that the matter be referred to the standing committee. That is what they are for. Another thing is this. Should the government decide to refer this matter to the committee, these organizations would have the opportunity of coming before the committee and there presenting their submissions.
It must not be considered that only the farm organizations would come. They would come, naturally, but there are other interests which might oppose the bill and would be welcome to present their submissions. Other organizations, such as industrial organizations, may oppose the bill. I do not know of any that do, but there may be some. Even the banks could make representations. Even other lending institutions could make representations.
So the standing committee, which according to the ratio of members in this house would have a majority of supporters of the government party of this house anyway, could hear all those submissions. Indeed, there could have been an expression of the opinions of the people of Canada who are interested in this measure. But the government says no.
When the hon. member for Acadia made the suggestion, which was most reasonable, the Minister of . Finance leaned over and 
spoke to the parliamentary assistant, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce walked in and sat with them. The three of them got into a little huddle. I have that in my notes here, because I drew three little heads with some hair on. After the huddle the minister rose and interrupted my hon. friend without even hearing the rest of his arguments, and said simply that the answer was no.
When I was a boy I went to Sunday school. As a teenager I was in a young lads' glee club. The director of that glee club taught us many songs, one of which-rather a unique one, but a good one, and we sang it with great gusto-was entitled "Have courage, my boy, to say no."
Walter was in the same club.
The verses were all about the wiles of the devil and the sins that beset young men. Each verse ended-and my, how we sang it-with the words, "Have courage, my boy, to say no."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On a question of privilege, I insist that the hon. member should not refer to one of his party as a devil.

I do not want to imply that one of my party is a devil but, frankly, I must admit that sometimes I think I have a little trace of him myself. However, I think the minister must have gone to Sunday school and learned that song, "Have courage, my boy, to say no." I should have imagined, with the minister sponsoring the bill, the government would be the first body that would want to hear representations from various organizations. I should have imagined they would be in a stronger position if they could say, "Yes, we shall send this bill to the committee and we shall hear what the various interested people have to say about it." I do not know why they do not say that.
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) spoke yesterday. I have a high regard for the hon. member. I do not laugh as much as some do when the hon. member speaks. He has a case to present, and his position over the years has been most difficult.
I say with all sincerity that I have a high regard for the hon. member for Rosthern. Yesterday he rose and spoke to this motion. He read from documents signed by various organizations and attempted to prove that the measure that is before the house is the very thing these organizations wanted. I am not saying whether or not it is, but if that is so then why not send the bill to the committee? Then we would find out whether or not that is exactly what these organizations want.
I am afraid, and I rather suspect, one reason the minister will not allow this bill to

go to the committee is that he knows these organizations will come down and say, "No, the interpretation the hon. member for Rosthern is putting forward is not the right interpretation." I have a suspicion that is exactly what the organizations would do, and of course the government would not want that to happen.
We would have voted for the bill. We voted for the resolution. When the bill was introduced it was a lot harsher than we ever expected it would be. We felt determined to vote against it. Yet we have said no; it might be well for the farmers to be able to get their loans and to have the banks guaranteed against loss, so perhaps we had better vote for the measure. Then came the amendment presented by our C.C.F. friends. Well, that posed a question for us. We had to make a decision. Were we going to vote for this amendment? We said it was a technical want of confidence motion, but there is a middle of the road proposition we can make so that we do not have to vote for that technical want of confidence motion. We said we would act as mediators. We would propose that the government itself send the bill to the committee, so we can vote confidence in the government and in the bill.
That was most reasonable, was it not? The minister rose and had the courage to say no. Now what faces us? We are faced with a decision now, as the hon. member for Acadia has said. Are we going to vote confidence in a measure and in a government that refuses to hear the representations of the people who would have been permitted to come before a proper standing committee, set up for that purpose, and present their wishes? The government can make their decision. They will still have a majority of members on the committee. They could make their decision on the basis of the evidence submitted. We feel that is a most reasonable request.
Now the picture has changed. Can we have confidence in a measure and in a government that does not want to hear the representations of these people on this measure? Any government that does not want to let the light shine in on its administration does not deserve a confidence vote of this house. I am afraid, therefore, as the hon. member for Acadia has said, that we will have to vote for this technical non-confidence motion and vote against the bill on second reading.

I do not like this Bill No. 82, Mr. Speaker, any more than 67509-78
Grain
other hon. members, but I do not like it for different reasons. This bill is entitled:
An act to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain.
That is not the problem in my constituency. We have not any grain to deliver. Here we have the government going out to help people who have grain and forgetting about the people who have had no crop for two years. I think that is disgraceful. I appealed to the government last year, and I appeal this year, to do something for these people.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What you want is advances on grain.

We could not get advances on grain because we have no grain, but you could do something for us. Help is needed in the interlake country. It is really bad there. I have tried to tell the government and the ministers what the situation is, but they think my language is too strong. They think I am exaggerating. These people in the interlake country are suffering. They are leaving their farms, and where are they going? They are going into the cities to compete with the men who are working there. That is a bad situation. If you lose a crop one year that is a calamity, but when you lose crops for two years that is a disaster. Certainly some of the people in the interlake country have a crop, but there are people there who will not be able to pay their taxes this year who have paid their taxes consistently for over 40 years.
I suggested that something should be done to bring in feed and seed to these people. I do not want to be told I am out of order, Mr. Speaker, but this is a serious matter and something ought to be done about it. I know I cannot move an amendment because it would call for the expenditure of money. It is going to cost money. There is more grain in the west than you know what to do with, and surely you could send some of that to the interlake country so some of these people will remain on their farms. An amendment of some kind could be introduced.
I could talk about this until tomorrow morning. I rose at this time to draw your attention to the serious situation there. Do not fail the people in the interlake country. They need help and need it badly. The unfortunate thing is that when I meet some of the cabinet ministers in the Manitoba government they say, "Well, what is the federal government doing?" Then when I speak to some of you gentlemen here you say, "Well what is the premier of Manitoba doing about it?" You are passing the buck. Don't do that. Don't do that to good citizens of Manitoba.

Grain
I am not going to say any more. I appeal to you as I have never appealed before. These people are in desperate circumstances. Do something for them.

The motion before the house is very simple, Mr. Speaker. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Kindersley requests that instead of giving this bill second reading the subject matter thereof be submitted to the committee on agriculture and colonization. One would have expected that the government would have been very anxious to accept that motion, because it provides them with an excellent opportunity to get off the hook.
As the debate has proceeded on this bill it has become evident that the members of the government and the private members supporting the government who come from the prairie provinces have been becoming more restless and resentful as time went on. It is not altogether because of what has been said on this side of the house but because I suspect they are beginning to hear from back home. They are beginning to find that the assumption with which they started out, namely that they could present this half-baked measure as a substitute for cash advances and get away with it, was wrong. They are beginning to find that the farmers in the prairie provinces are simply not going to take this matter lying down. Hence the desire seems to be there to hurry it through, rush it through the house without too much comment, in the hope that it will be a forgotten matter before very long.
Recent events here have shown that they are not getting away with that idea. I want to say that we certainly welcome the change of attitude on the part of our Progressive Conservative friends to the right and of our Social Credit friends to the left.
There is no change in attitude; merely clarification.

I will explain that remark in a moment. I refer to the fact that, on the part of both of those parties, those who spoke for them had announced that they were going to vote for second reading of this bill. They have now both announced that they are going to oppose the second reading of this bill and vote for the amendment to refer this matter to a committee. That is a change of attitude.
No; merely clarification.

The change is perfectly justified, and I say that not in any criticism. I say it rather as a compliment to their good judgment in having at last swung in behind the C.C.F. on this question.

What are some of the reasons why we have asked that the subject matter of this bill should be referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization? Perhaps the main reason is the fact that the hon. member for Rosthern, on two occasions at least and perhaps three in this debate, has risen in this house and attempted to put his own interpretation on what happened at the Saskatoon grain conference. As one of those who were present at that conference, I am quite satisfied that the interpretation he seeks to place upon the desire of the delegates who attended that conference is not the correct one.
Naturally I do not expect him to agree with me but certainly he can go along this far. If he contends that what the delegates at the Saskatoon conference-and consequently the smaller delegation which was sent by this conference to interview the government- asked for is what is now contained in the bill, whereas of course we argue that it is not, then would it not be the wisest course for the sake of his own argument to submit this matter to the committee on agriculture and colonization and invite these various farm organizations which composed this conference to send their delegates again to Ottawa and have them place their wishes before that committee? Surely that would settle the argument as to what they asked for.
We contend that they did not ask for bank loans at 5 per cent, and voluminous evidence has been placed on the record to prove our contention. All that the hon. member for Rosthern has had to go on so far has been a set of resolutions passed at the Saskatoon grain conference which, because of the fact that they were not too specific in every respect, gave him just enough elbow room to place his own interpretation on them. We are willing to place our argument before that committee, and we are willing to hear the representations of these various farm organizations before that committee. Nothing could be more reasonable than that.
When one looks at this bill and hears the speeches of the members supporting it, one begins to wonder whether they are talking about the bill because, according to some of the speeches that have been made in support of this legislation, one would get the impression that the government is acceding to the request of the farm organizations for cash advances and that proposition, of course, is what the hon. member for Rosthern continues to argue. But what does this bill do? It does not provide for cash advances to the farmers. All it does is provide a guarantee to the banks in the event that they should make some loans. Not only does it do that; it also

Grain
provides for penalties to farmers in case they should misunderstand the legislation.
I think that is one of the features of the bill that would come as rather a surprise to a good many farmers. I think they will be surprised when they read the bill and find that if they happen to fill out the form which is supplied to them through the banks in the wrong way, or if they happen to make a mistake-and that would not be too hard, considering the fact that the government has set up regulations even before the legislation is passed-they are liable to a fine of $500. That is a far different thing from cash advances. It is an attempt to shift from the government to the banks the responsibility for the financing of agriculture in this crisis. It is also an attempt to shift the cost of that operation from the government to the shoulders of the farmers themselves.
In view of all that, it is rather strange to hear the word "misrepresentation" used by the hon. member for Rosthern and others. The bill itself is a complete misrepresentation of what the Saskatoon grain conference asked for and of what was asked for by every farm organization and every chamber of commerce plus the retail merchants plus anybody else who has had anything to say about it living in western Canada. It misses the point completely. It does not fulfil the functions for which cash advances were intended.
It does more than that. This attempt by the government to get out from under, to shift the responsibility for a crisis which is of their own making on to the banking system of this country, is doing more damage to the
whole philosophy of the principles of orderly marketing than anything I can remember that has been done in this house previously.
Let us consider the situation. In 1946 the farmers were told that in order to enter into an agreement for the sale of grain under which Canada could guarantee a supply of grain to our customers, two things were needed. One was that the farmers would have to agree to a ceiling price, and it was set at $1.55. The second was that all the grain must be handled through the wheat board in order that there might be stability of price and stability of supply. The grain producers in this country were quite conscious of the fact that the market price at that time was higher than the amount provided in the agreement with Britain. However, they went along with the government on the understanding that the government was assuming the responsibility for the marketing of that grain. Today the government is denying that responsibility.
